meta.name: Shih Tzu Cost Year 1: $2,500–$5,000 (Real Budget)
meta.excerpt: Shih Tzus are a small breed with modest food and exercise costs — but professional grooming is a non-negotiable recurring expense, and their brachycephalic structure creates specific vet costs to plan for. Here are the real numbers.
meta.meta_description: Shih Tzu first-year cost: $2,500–$5,000. Real numbers for puppy price, vet care, professional grooming every 4–6 weeks, and dental care for this small breed.

hero.alt: Adult Shih Tzu relaxing at home in a family setting

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What a Shih Tzu Really Costs in Its First Year
intro.html:
Buy a Shih Tzu from a health-tested breeder and the first-year bill typically lands between $2,500 and $5,000, with the puppy price itself ($1,000–$2,500) responsible for most of that spread. Adopt instead ($200–$500 through a rescue, often already vaccinated and altered) and the same first year settles closer to $1,800–$3,200. Set against a large-breed puppy, the food and baseline vet numbers stay small — a 9–16 lb adult eats a fraction of what a Labrador does — but this is a breed where the expense that never shrinks isn't food. It's the coat.

A Shih Tzu's floor-length, continuously growing coat is the breed's signature look, and it comes with a signature bill: a professional groom every 6–8 weeks at $55–$90 a visit, which adds up to $360–$720 a year, every year, for the dog's entire life. Combine that with a lifespan that runs 10 to 18 years — genuinely long for a toy breed — and grooming becomes one of the largest cumulative expenses of ownership, easily outpacing food and rivaling or beating routine vet care most years. Over a 14-year life, that's $5,000–$10,000 spent on haircuts alone, a number worth sitting with before you commit.

The second cost driver specific to this breed is its flattened face. It's a much milder version of what you'd see in a Bulldog or French Bulldog, but it's still real: prominent, slightly protruding eyes prone to ulcers and dry eye, a shortened muzzle that makes heat harder to shed than it is for a non-brachycephalic dog, and facial skin folds that need wiping every few days to prevent infection. None of it is optional upkeep. Skip the daily eye wipe and the weekly face-fold check and you trade a cheap grooming supply for an expensive vet visit.

What Actually Drives the Number

  • The puppy purchase ($1,000–$2,500) is the single largest item in year one — and then it never recurs.
  • Professional grooming ($360–$720/yr) is the cost that separates a Shih Tzu budget from a short-coated toy breed's budget, and it's permanent.
  • Pet insurance runs on the higher side for a small dog — $350–$600 rather than the $250–$400 you'd see for a breed without eye and airway risk.
  • Food and exercise costs stay low: 20–30 minutes of daily activity, no yard requirement, and small daily portions keep this part of the budget modest for the dog's whole life.

Because the Shih Tzu was bred purely for companionship rather than work, almost every recurring cost in this breed's life scales down compared to sporting or working dogs of similar price point — except the one tied directly to its coat and its face. Budget those two honestly and the rest of the first year is genuinely manageable, even on a modest income.

cost.label: Full Breakdown
cost.heading: Every Dollar, From Setup Through Month Twelve
cost.html:
One-Time Setup Costs

A Shih Tzu doesn't need heavy-duty gear — it's a gentle, low-drive toy breed that won't test a crate's weld or chew through a leash in a week. The items worth spending real money on are the grooming tools, since they'll be in daily or near-daily use from day one.

ItemCostNotes
Puppy (health-tested breeder)$1,000–$2,500Ask for OFA hip and patella clearances on both parents, a CAER eye exam, and family history on renal dysplasia
Rescue / adoption$200–$500Usually includes altering and vaccines; adult rescue Shih Tzus often arrive with known temperament and some house manners already in place
Crate (small/medium)$35–$80A 9–16 lb adult only needs a medium; buy the final size and use a divider for puppyhood
Bed$25–$70Not typically a destructive chewer, so it's fine to buy something comfortable rather than indestructible
Grooming tool kit$40–$70Pin brush, metal comb, and detangling spray; used every 2–3 days minimum, so don't buy the cheapest option
Eye and face care supplies$15–$30The daily eye-wipe habit starts the day the puppy arrives — have these on hand before homecoming
Bowls, collar, leash, ID tag$35–$70Small-breed sizing; a flat collar set shallow enough that facial hair doesn't tangle in it
Baby gate / exercise pen$25–$70Check bar spacing carefully — a Shih Tzu puppy is small enough to squeeze through gates rated for bigger dogs

The First Twelve Months, Month by Month

Costs aren't evenly spread across the year — they front-load hard, then flatten out.

  • Months 1–3: The puppy fee or adoption fee, every setup item in the table above, the first vet exam and vaccine series, and possibly spay/neuter if the breeder didn't already do it ($200–$400). This is the single most expensive stretch of the whole year.
  • Months 4–6: Vaccine boosters finish, the first professional groom happens around month 3–4 as the puppy coat starts matting, and a puppy class ($150–$250) is worth starting now — housetraining is still in progress and toy breeds commonly need 4–6 months to become reliable.
  • Months 7–12: Costs settle into a rhythm — a grooming appointment every 6–8 weeks, monthly flea/tick/heartworm prevention, and routine care. Insurance premiums, if started early, are now paying off as the dog ages into the window where eye and joint issues start to show up.

Feeding a 9–16 lb Dog

A Shih Tzu at adult weight eats roughly ¾ to 1 cup of small-breed kibble a day, split across two meals. A quality small-bag (4–6 lb) of premium food runs longer per dollar than it looks on the shelf price alone, simply because the daily volume is so low — a single bag can last four to six weeks for one dog. Puppies eat a puppy-specific formula through roughly the first 9–10 months (toy breeds mature faster than large breeds), then transition to adult food; the annual food total of $200–$400 reflects this small-portion reality and is one of the lowest line items in the entire budget, puppy or adult.

Ongoing Annual Costs

ExpenseAnnual CostNotes
Food (small-breed premium)$200–$400One of the lowest food costs of any breed on this site
Vet (routine)$300–$600Puppy year adds the vaccine series and possibly spay/neuter at $200–$400 if not done pre-purchase
Professional grooming$360–$720$55–$90 per session, every 6–8 weeks; the standout recurring cost of this breed
Flea/tick/heartworm prevention$80–$150Small-breed dosing keeps this well below what a large dog costs
Pet insurance$350–$600Above average for a toy breed because of eye and airway risk; enroll before any diagnosis exists
Eye and face care supplies$50–$100The daily wipe routine consumes wipes and tear-stain remover steadily over the year
Puppy classes (year one)$150–$250Housetraining-focused classes pay off given the 4–6 month timeline typical for this breed
Year One Total (breeder puppy)$2,500–$5,000+Ongoing years: $1,200–$2,200 without emergencies

Budget Path vs. Premium Path

Budget-conscious, still responsible ($2,500–$2,900): Rescue or a modestly priced ethical breeder toward the lower end ($1,000–$1,500), basic setup gear at the low end of each range, learning some at-home grooming maintenance between professional visits, a wellness-focused insurance plan, and group puppy classes rather than private training.

Premium path ($4,200–$5,000+): A puppy from a breeder doing full health screening at the higher end ($2,000–$2,500), a full grooming appointment cadence at $80–$90 a visit, comprehensive accident-and-illness insurance from week one, and private or semi-private training sessions layered on top of group classes. Both paths produce a healthy, well-adjusted dog — the difference is upfront screening depth, coverage breadth, and convenience, not welfare.

health.label: Emergency Costs
health.heading: The Bills This Breed's Face and Frame Create
health.html:
A Shih Tzu can live anywhere from 10 to 18 years, and that flattened face and small, delicate frame create a specific set of vulnerabilities that a flat-faced sporting or working breed simply doesn't have to plan for. Most of these are manageable with routine care; a subset require surgery. Knowing the price tags ahead of time is what makes the insurance decision easy rather than reactive.

ConditionTypical CostNotes
BOAS surgery (airway correction)$1,500–$4,000Widens nostrils and shortens the soft palate for dogs with real breathing restriction; not every Shih Tzu needs it, but symptomatic dogs benefit enormously
Eye conditions (corneal ulcer, dry eye, proptosis)$200–$1,500+Prominent eyes make ulcers a real risk; chronic dry eye (KCS) needs lifelong twice-daily drops at $40–$80/month ($480–$960/yr); proptosis, where the eye dislocates from the socket, is a same-day surgical emergency
Patellar luxation surgery$1,500–$4,000 per kneeCommon in toy breeds generally; mild grades are managed conservatively, moderate to severe grades often need orthopedic repair
Renal dysplasia management$500–$3,000+/yrA kidney development disorder that shows up disproportionately in this breed and can lead to early renal failure; managed with prescription renal diet and medication — ask about family history before buying
Hip dysplasia$500–$3,000More common in toy breeds than most owners expect; OFA screening in the parents lowers the odds meaningfully

Why This Breed's Risk Profile Shapes the Insurance Decision

Renal dysplasia and dry eye are the two conditions that make Shih Tzu insurance math different from a healthier-coated toy breed. Renal dysplasia is a congenital condition — meaning a policy started after any early bloodwork flags kidney values will likely exclude it, so timing matters as much as coverage breadth. Dry eye is the opposite problem: it's not usually congenital, but once diagnosed it's a permanent pre-existing condition for insurance purposes, and the $480–$960 a year in drops adds up over a potential 10–18 year lifespan into a five-figure lifetime number. Enrolling in a policy during the puppy's first healthy months, before either condition can be flagged, is the only way coverage for these two issues actually functions the way it's supposed to.

Breeding-side screening also affects your odds directly. A breeder who provides OFA hip and patella clearances on both parents plus a current CAER eye exam is filtering out a meaningful share of the conditions in the table above before you even bring the puppy home. It's reasonable to pay more upfront for that paperwork — it's cheaper, in expectation, than the alternative.

special.label: Watch Out
special.heading: The Costs Owners Underestimate Going In
special.html:
Grooming: DIY Tools vs. the Professional Schedule

The most common financial miscalculation new owners make is budgeting for professional grooming once and then forgetting it recurs every 6–8 weeks for the entire life of the dog. At $55–$90 a session, that's $360–$720 a year — and over a long 10–18 year lifespan, $5,000–$10,000 in grooming spend before you account for anything else. A one-time DIY tool kit (pin brush, metal comb, detangling spray, and eventually a set of clippers for face and paw touch-ups) runs $40–$100 and can stretch the interval between professional visits or reduce the scope of each visit, but it does not eliminate the need for them — the coat still mats in the armpits and behind the ears if brushing lapses even a few days, and an inexperienced full-body clip at home risks nicks and uneven patches that a groomer then has to fix anyway.

Regional Price Swings

Grooming and vet pricing both move with geography more than most first-time owners expect. A puppy cut that costs $55 in a smaller Midwest or Southern city can run $85–$90 in a dense coastal metro, and routine vet exam fees follow a similar pattern — urban clinics with higher overhead often price 20–30% above suburban or rural practices for the same service. If you're near the top of a metro area, budget toward the higher end of every range in this guide rather than the midpoint.

Money-Saving Moves That Don't Cut Corners on Welfare

  • Learn basic between-visit maintenance — sanitary trims, paw pad hair, and face touch-ups — to stretch a groomer visit from 6 weeks to 8 without letting mats form.
  • Buy grooming and eye-care supplies in bulk rather than replacing them one at a time; wipes, comb spray, and tear-stain solution all keep well and cost less per unit bought in quantity.
  • Enroll in insurance the week the puppy comes home rather than after the first vet visit — this is the single biggest lever on lifetime cost given how much of this breed's risk (dry eye, renal dysplasia) is timing-sensitive for coverage.
  • Choose a group puppy class over one-on-one training for general obedience and housetraining support; it's a fraction of the private-session cost and this breed's main training challenge is patience with a small bladder, not a behavioral problem needing individualized work.

One false economy specific to this breed: stretching grooming intervals past 8 weeks to save money. Once the coat mats close to the skin, the fix often isn't a trim — it's a full shave-down, which costs the same or more and leaves the dog exposed and uncomfortable until the coat regrows. The other is skipping insurance to save the $350–$600 premium; a single BOAS surgery or a year of renal dysplasia management costs several times that in a bad year.

Rescue vs. Breeder: The Real Cost Gap

The $1,800–$3,200 rescue path saves real money mainly by removing the $1,000–$2,500 purchase price and often bundling in vaccines and altering that would otherwise cost $200–$400. What it doesn't remove is the grooming line item — a rescued Shih Tzu still needs the same $360–$720 a year in professional coat care, and if the dog arrives already matted or neglected, the first grooming appointment can run considerably higher than the routine rate to deal with pelted fur safely. Adult rescues also sometimes arrive with known health history, which can shortcut some of the guesswork breeder buyers do through genetic testing and clearances — worth asking about directly with the rescue organization.

Housetraining: A Time Cost, Not Just a Dollar Cost

Toy breeds have small bladders relative to their body size, and Shih Tzus commonly need 4–6 months of consistent scheduling before they're reliably housetrained — noticeably longer than most medium or large breeds. This isn't a huge line item financially (enzyme cleaner and the occasional belly band add up to modest amounts), but it's a genuine lifestyle cost: someone needs to be available for a consistent bathroom schedule for the better part of half a year. Factor this into the decision the same way you'd factor in a dollar figure — it's a real commitment, just not one that shows up on a receipt.

faq.q: Why does Shih Tzu grooming cost more than for other small breeds?
faq.a: Because the coat grows continuously and never stops needing professional shaping — unlike a Chihuahua or Pug, whose short coats are essentially wash-and-go for life. A Shih Tzu needs a trim every 6–8 weeks or the coat mats, particularly under the arms and behind the ears, which can become painful and even trap moisture against the skin. This isn't a luxury add-on; it's baked into the breed. Budget $360–$720 a year as a fixed, recurring cost that doesn't taper off as the dog ages.

faq.q: Can I lower grooming costs by clipping the coat myself?
faq.a: Partially, yes. Daily-to-every-2–3-day brushing is required regardless of who does the cutting, and learning simple maintenance trims around the face, paws, and sanitary area can stretch the gap between professional visits. Clipping the whole body yourself is possible with practice, but the learning curve is real, and a botched first attempt at home often costs you a corrective visit anyway. Most owners save the most by combining home maintenance with slightly longer, not skipped, professional visits.

faq.q: What's the costliest health condition to watch for in this breed?
faq.a: Renal dysplasia is the most serious long-term risk because it can trigger early kidney failure and needs ongoing prescription diet and medication, sometimes exceeding $3,000 a year. Dry eye (KCS) is the most consistently expensive because the twice-daily drops are lifelong at $40–$80 a month. BOAS airway surgery is the largest single bill if a dog develops significant breathing restriction. Insurance purchased in early puppyhood, before any of these can be flagged as pre-existing, is the most effective financial protection against all three.

faq.q: Are Shih Tzus a good fit for apartment living?
faq.a: Yes — this is genuinely one of the better toy breeds for smaller spaces. Daily exercise needs are modest (20–30 minutes total), they're not habitual barkers, and their temperament stays calm indoors. The two practical considerations are the grooming routine, which needs a bit of dedicated space and time at home, and the breed's dislike of being left alone for long stretches — they were bred as companion dogs and do best with someone around most of the day.

faq.q: Does the flat face affect exercise and heat-related costs?
faq.a: It affects exercise timing more than cost directly. Because Shih Tzus manage heat less efficiently than non-brachycephalic breeds, walks in hot or humid weather need to be shorter and scheduled for cooler parts of the day, and heavy exertion in heat should be avoided altogether. The financial angle shows up if this gets ignored — heat stress in a brachycephalic dog is an emergency vet visit, not a minor issue, so the real cost-saving move is simply respecting the breed's lower heat tolerance rather than pushing exercise on a hot afternoon.
